title: What Makes a Teacher: Everything I Wish I Learned in College
author: Melinda Karshner
summary: Melinda Karshner, a credentialed teacher with a master's degree from UC Irvine, reflects on what her excellent but incomplete preparation program failed to give her: any substantive knowledge of dyslexia, and a student teaching placement that left her to manage a class of 38 with a burned-out cooperating teacher. Her core argument is that teacher preparation programs are wrong not just in curriculum but in structure—student teaching is too short, too unsupported, and too easily treated as a favor to the institution rather than a learning experience for the candidate. She proposes a two-year model: year one mirrors rigorous coursework, and year two is a paid apprenticeship with a master teacher, focused entirely on classroom practice. The piece is notable for naming dyslexia as a gap no credential program should allow, given that it affects one in five students.
points: Even an outstanding credential program at UC Irvine omitted dyslexia entirely from its coursework—a gap Karshner argues is equivalent to training OBGYNs without covering perimenopause.
Student teaching as currently structured routinely places candidates with burned-out cooperating teachers, making the experience sink-or-swim rather than a genuine apprenticeship.

Karshner proposes a two-year preparation model: one year of coursework (including all current best-practice literacy content), followed by a paid, supervised apprenticeship with nothing else on the candidate's plate.
The piece identifies lesson planning, grading strategy, and reflective decision-making as concrete skills programs currently leave to chance.
Systemic dysfunction in student teaching placement—not just curriculum gaps—is identified as a primary reason good teacher candidates leave the profession before or shortly after it begins.
quotes: Nobody ever said the word dyslexia. Not once. Not in a single one of those genuinely science-based, best-practice reading courses.

Schools of education should teach dyslexia. Period. It is a reading disability that affects as many as one in five students, which means there is no version of a teaching career where you don't encounter it.

Leaving future teachers uneducated about what dyslexia is and how to address it as a tier one practitioner is the equivalent of the medical field declining to train OBGYNs in perimenopause and menopause care.

I was placed in a 6th grade classroom with 38 students. My cooperating teacher was burnt out beyond belief, and her friend stated bluntly that I had been assigned to help her. I wasn't there to learn. I was there to be a second adult in the room.

The more years I teach, the more convinced I become that we've built teacher preparation programs all wrong. Not just in what is taught, which is the loudest complaint these days, but in how they're structured.
Year two is student teaching, and nothing else. No additional coursework beyond protected time to sit with a master teacher one on one and actually learn the job.
